primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome due to MCT8 (SLC16A2) deficiency
mechanism: SLC16A2 encodes MCT8, a thyroid-hormone cell-membrane transporter important for T3 entry into neurons and across blood-brain-barrier endothelium. Loss of MCT8 reduces neuronal thyroid-hormone availability despite abnormal circulating thyroid-hormone concentrations.
vignette: A 2-year-old boy has severe developmental delay, truncal hypotonia, poor head control, dystonic movements, and little speech. His maternal uncle had a similar disorder. Laboratory studies show elevated serum T3 with relatively low T4. Genetic testing identifies a hemizygous loss-of-function variant in SLC16A2.
lead: Which of the following cellular abnormalities most directly explains this child's neurologic phenotype?
correct: Reduced transport of thyroid hormone across cell membranes into developing neurons
distractors: Reduced transcriptional response to T3 due to a dominant-negative thyroid hormone receptor beta
Failure of thyroid peroxidase to organify iodide in the thyroid follicular lumen
Reduced conversion of T4 to T3 by type 2 deiodinase within target tissues
Failure of the sodium-iodide symporter to concentrate iodide in thyroid follicular cells
distractor_notes: THRB resistance alters nuclear receptor signaling and produces a different thyroid phenotype; the stem identifies loss of the MCT8 transporter.
Thyroid peroxidase deficiency impairs hormone synthesis in the thyroid gland rather than membrane transport of hormone into neurons.
Deiodinase defects alter hormone conversion, not SLC16A2-mediated cell-membrane transport.
NIS defects impair thyroidal iodide uptake and hormone synthesis rather than tissue uptake of circulating thyroid hormone.
key_expl: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome is caused by SLC16A2 loss of function. SLC16A2 encodes MCT8, a thyroid-hormone membrane transporter with an important role in neuronal T3 uptake and thyroid-hormone passage through blood-brain-barrier endothelium. Reduced hormone entry into brain cells disrupts thyroid-hormone-dependent neurodevelopment even though circulating T3 may be elevated.
objective: Explain the neurologic phenotype of MCT8 deficiency as impaired thyroid-hormone transport into developing brain cells.
clues: high T3 with relatively low T4
